title: Judas Iscariot walked beside Jesus, heard His voice, saw the blind see and the dead rise, yet his story ends in darkness, and that tension forces a question that refuses to stay quiet: did he lose salvation, or was it never his to begin with?
paragraphs: Judas Iscariot walked beside Jesus, heard His voice, saw the blind see and the dead rise, yet his story ends in darkness, and that tension forces a question that refuses to stay quiet: did he lose salvation, or was it never his to begin with?

The weight of that question is not academic; it presses on the soul. Because if someone could follow Christ so closely and still fall away, what does that mean for you? You remember moments when truth was clear, when conviction stirred, when you knew. God saw it. You knew. And still, you hesitated.

Scripture does not leave Judas undefined. Jesus Himself speaks with unsettling clarity. In John 6:64, it says, “But there are some of you who do not believe.” Then it adds, “For Jesus knew from the beginning who those were who did not believe, and who it was who would betray him.” Read that again. From the beginning. Judas was present, but he was not believing.

This is where many struggle. Judas performed ministry. He was sent out with the others, preached, cast out demons, handled the money. On the surface, nothing separated him from the rest. But here is the fracture beneath the appearance: proximity to Jesus is not the same as faith in Jesus.

But here’s what most people don’t realize. Jesus called Judas “a devil” in John 6:70. Not someone who would become lost, but someone already defined by unbelief. The betrayal did not create his condition; it revealed it. The hidden root surfaced in a moment of pressure.

Yet there is another side that must be faced honestly. Judas felt remorse. Matthew 27:3 says he was filled with regret. He returned the silver. He confessed, “I have sinned by betraying innocent blood.” But remorse is not repentance. One turns you inward in despair; the other turns you toward God in surrender.

Peter also failed. He denied Jesus three times. But Peter ran back in tears that led to restoration. Judas ran into isolation that led to death. Two men, two failures, two very different roots. One was broken toward God. The other was exposed without transformation.

So did Judas lose salvation? Scripture never shows him possessing saving faith to begin with. Jesus says in John 17:12, “None of them has been lost except the son of destruction, that the Scripture might be fulfilled.” He was not described as saved and then lost, but as set apart for a role that exposed his true nature.

And that should unsettle you in the right way. Because this is not just about Judas. It is about the terrifying possibility of external religion without internal surrender. Sitting near truth, speaking truth, even serving in its name, while your heart remains untouched.

You don’t drift into that by accident. It happens in small compromises, quiet justifications, hidden affections. Money meant more to Judas than the Master. Thirty pieces of silver exposed what sermons could not fix. What is your silver? What do you protect when God confronts you?

Here is the dividing line. True salvation produces perseverance because it is sustained by grace, not human strength. As Ephesians 2:8 declares, “For by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God.” A gift is received, not performed. And what God gives, He sustains.

Judas stands as a warning, not that true believers can be accidentally lost, but that false assurance can live dangerously close to holy things. You can kiss Jesus like Judas did and still not love Him. That is the danger. That is the mirror.
Because there is still a different ending available to you right now.

Turn while your heart is still responsive. Come to Christ not as a performer, but as a sinner in need of mercy. He does not reject the one who truly comes. He receives, cleanses, restores. But the window is not something you control forever.
Say it plainly: I don’t want to be close to Jesus and still lost. Let that confession break something open.
Follow this path deeper. Stay where truth keeps cutting and healing at the same time. Save this so you remember the difference when your heart starts drifting again.
